newsitem.title: JAPAN: Volume of dollar-yen futures surges on TIFFE.
newsitem.headline: Volume of dollar-yen futures surges on TIFFE.

text.p: The Tokyo International Financial Futures Exchange (TIFFE) said on Wednesday that its trading volume for dollar-yen currency futures surged more than five-fold in the last business year, boosted by the weaker yen and growing involvement in the market by commodity brokers.
The exchange said traded volume jumped to 57,190 contracts in the year to March 31, 1997 from 10,733 a year earlier.

A TIFFE spokesman attributed the surge to the yen's continued decline against the dollar and to growing use of derivatives by commodities brokers to hedge risk. Traders also cited speculative interest by individual investors operating through commodity brokers.

Five new commodities brokerage houses joined the exchange as non-clearing members during the year, a TIFFE spokesman said. There has been growing participation in the market by commodities brokers in the last few years, with the first broker joining in 1995 although the dollar-yen currency futures contract was listed in 1989.

The dollar-yen currency futures contract is becoming popular among commodities futures brokers as an instrument to manage currency risk, for example when trading yen-denominated precious metals in the domestic markets, the spokesman said.
But traders said growing participation by individual investors via these commodities brokers was behind the sharp increase in the trading volume.

Ha Sangsoon, general manager of the asset management department at Ace Koeki Co Ltd, a major Japanese commodities brokerage house, said there is steady demand from retail investors who want to trade the contract for speculative purposes.

"It seems to me that about 80 percent of individual investors trade the contract for speculative reasons. The rest are those who use the contract to hedge their positions in the commodities markets," he said.
Sangsoon said commodities brokers have urged other members, namely banks and securities houses, to make more frequent use of the contract to raise liquidity, but in vain.

The interbank forward market is the key trading arena for big foreign-exchange players, mainly dealer banks and their multinational corporate customers who are accustomed to dealing in lots of one million dollars or more.
The forward market operates on a one-to-one basis, while currency futures are traded in standardised contract terms at a much lower cost.
TIFFE introduced an evening session for the currency futures contract from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. (0700 GMT to 0900 GMT) in March to encourage greater participation by bigger players.

TIFFE, founded in 1989, specialises in futures contracts for currencies and interest rates. Other TIFFEE contracts include three-month Euroyen interest rate futures and options, one-year Euroyen interest rate futures and three-month Eurodollar interest rate futures. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-33432-8570
